  (`pm-schedule-approval`, `replacement-schedule-approval`, `qnn-notifications`,
  `guest-cleaning-requests`, `block-change-approval`, `stage-interlock`,
  `pm-schedule-settings`). **All seven defs were removed with the Phase 0 domain
  strip** — `grep "moduleKey: '<key>'" config/defs/` returns nothing for each — so
  no `/api/config/dynamic/<key>` route was ever registered and every section on
  the page read and wrote an endpoint that does not exist.
- `system_config` holds **0 rows** for all seven keys, so nothing configured was
  lost by removing the only screen that could edit them.

Also removed with it: the `roleAssignmentKeys` suppression set in
`config/index.tsx`, which existed to keep those keys out of the auto-discovered
"Additional Modules" section. With no defs behind any of its nine entries
(the seven above plus `filter-cleaning-reasons` and `filter-field-options`) it
was filtering nothing.

Routes 49 → 48; `routes/config/*.tsx` 25 → 24.

The `filter-data-management` remnants went with it (operator request, same day).
Three places named a module that the Phase 0 strip removed:

- `EXPLICIT_GRANT_KEYS` in `config/index.tsx` — the allow-list of Super Admin cards
  a non-admin could be granted. Its only member matched no card, so every
  non-admin already saw an empty section; `visibleSuperAdminCards` is now simply
  SUPER_ADMIN-or-nothing. **How to delegate a card again is written at the call

- `EXTRA_MODULES` in `access-matrix.tsx` — a SYNTHETIC "Filter Data Management"

- `HIDDEN_MODULE_KEYS` in the same file — the same seven Role Assignments keys,
  with a comment telling the reader to keep it in sync with a set that no longer

No stored grants were affected: `system_config['access-matrix']` holds only

## [Unreleased] - Per-role instrument attribute access (2026-08-19)

Attributes no longer ride on `INSTRUMENT_UPDATE` alone. One administered rule per
role decides which attributes it may change, whether a password is needed, and
every change now carries a mandatory remark.

- **Config → Roles & Access → Attribute Access** (new tab). Four states per role:
  *not configured* (inherits Edit Instruments — the old behaviour), *all editable*,
  *all view-only*, *selected editable and the rest view-only*, plus a per-role
  "ask for the operator's password on every attribute change".
- **Schema**: `role_configs.attribute_access` JSONB, nullable, no default —
  shipping this changes nothing for anyone until a rule is set. Migration
  `20260819120000_role_attribute_access`, hand-authored (the three destructive
  statements `migrate diff` emits here are stripped and named in its header),
  applied to `compliance_core_db_test` as well, drift guard PASS. Model and enum
  counts unchanged: 34 / 13.
- **Editable means change, add and remove.** A view-only role gets no Edit, no
  Delete and no Add. In SELECTED mode only the named keys carry Edit/Delete;
  adding a NEW key stays allowed, because a new key cannot overwrite a protected
  one.
- **Mandatory remarks** to change or delete a recorded value, recorded on the
  audit row's `reason`. NOT on a first fill — that is registration, and demanding
  a reason on every key of a new instrument teaches people to type "x". One
  dialog serves both acts and shows the before and after, so the remark is
  written against the real change.
- **The rule NARROWS `INSTRUMENT_UPDATE` and never widens it.** A role without
  Edit Instruments stays read-only whatever mode is stored, and the tab says so
  rather than offering a setting that would do nothing.
- **Enforced server-side** in one shared gate used by POST, PUT and DELETE, with
  the decision itself in `@digilog/shared` so the panel renders exactly what the
  API allows. Access is checked BEFORE the password prompt: a refused write never
  costs a re-authentication.
- An unrecognised stored rule is treated as *unconfigured*, never as a grant.

**Caught by its own tests:** the PUT stored the key list even under ALL_EDIT /
ALL_VIEW, where it is inert — until someone switched the role back to SELECTED
and a list nobody had looked at in months quietly became the rule. The tab
cleared it client-side; the endpoint now does too.

**Contract change for existing callers:** `PUT /:id/attributes/:key` and
`DELETE /:id/attributes/:key` now require `reason`, and `POST /:id/attributes`
requires it when it overwrites an existing value. A missing remark is a 400 from
the body schema, which runs before the handler — so it is answered without
confirming whether the instrument exists.

## [Unreleased] - Limit and range attributes follow the decimals attributes (2026-08-19)

A limit or a range is a reading, so it is now shown at the same precision as the
reading it bounds — "27 breached > 25" reads as a bug in the comparison when the
column beside it says 27.0.

- **Two new key lists in Telemetry Keys config**: which attribute keys hold a
  temperature, and which a humidity. Shipped filled with every Limit and Range key
  in use. Administered rather than matched on the word "temp": these keys are
  operator-typed and already inconsistent here (`High Temperature` and
  `High Temperature Limit` both live), a word rule would wrongly claim any future
  key containing those letters, and a wrong guess is then fixed by editing config
  instead of shipping code.
- **`GET /api/instruments/:id/attributes`** annotates each row with `slot`,
  `decimals` and `display`. Resolved server-side so this panel, the set-point
  column and the alarm row cannot quote one limit three ways.
- **`display` is presentation; `value` is the record.** The panel renders
  `display`, but Edit opens on the STORED value — saving a formatted string would
  rewrite a §11 record to match a display choice. A classified key holding
  something unparseable ("about 25") keeps its raw value rather than blanking.
- The room chart's limit header is formatted too, at the decimals the room's
  instruments agree on.

On live data with `temp_decimals=2` / `humid_decimals=5` set on DEMO-TH-361: its
`High Temperature Limit` 25 renders 25.00 and `High Humidity Range` 100 renders
100.00000, while CWH-01 (no decimals attribute) shows 23.0 at the site default.

## [Unreleased] - Set point follows the instrument's own limits (2026-08-19)

The dashboard's SET POINT column read the ROOM's limits while the alarm evaluator
enforced the INSTRUMENT's limit attributes — two specs for one instrument. On this
database that was not theoretical: every instrument carrying limits was unplaced,
and both placed instruments carried none, so the column read NA for exactly the
instruments an alarm could fire for.

`buildTelemetryOverview` now resolves the band through the SAME `alarm-limits`
config and `limitsFor()` resolver the evaluator uses: the instrument's own limits
where it declares any, else its room's. Rows gain `limitSource`
(`INSTRUMENT | ROOM | null`), shown as a tooltip on the set-point cells.

Two decisions worth keeping:
- **Wholesale, never mixed bound-by-bound.** "Room says 18–25, instrument declares
  a high of 23, so show 18–23" looks friendlier and reintroduces the bug: the
  evaluator reads only the instrument's attributes, so nothing would fire below 18
  while the table painted that cell red. An undeclared bound is UNBOUNDED, exactly
  as the evaluator treats it.
- **An inverted pair resolves to no band**, matching `checkPair` raising nothing
  for it. A range no reading can satisfy is a misconfiguration, not a permanent
  breach.

Also fixed, so no surface is left on the old source:
- The floorplan room chips judged out-of-spec against `room.tempMin/Max` read
  straight off the plan while the row's status came from the resolved band, so a
  chip could sit green on a reading the same instrument's row called out of spec.
  Both now use the one resolved band.
- The room chart's in-spec band was the ROOM's. A room chart overlays every
  instrument in it, and they can now each carry their own limits — one band
  belonging to only some of the lines reads as applying to all of them. It is now
  drawn only where every instrument in the room AGREES; where they differ the
  header says so and no band is shaded. With no overview row yet it still falls
  back to the room's bound, which is the only thing known at that moment.
- The unplaced tray said those instruments "cannot be checked against limits".
  False as of this change — it is the headline case.

Effect on live data: CWH-01 now shows 18–23 °C (its own `High Temperature`), and
CWH-02 turns OUT_OF_SPEC at 71 %RH against its own 40–60 — an excursion the
dashboard previously had no limits to detect.

## [Unreleased] - Instrument attributes: one list (2026-08-19)

The Attributes panel showed recorded attributes in a table and the profile's
unset keys in a separate dashed block below it. Two lists of the same kind of
thing, so a key typed on the instrument looked like it had landed somewhere other
than the profile's keys. They are now interleaved in ONE table — profile order
first (it reads like the registration form), then any key this instrument alone
carries.

What the merge deliberately keeps:
- **"Not set" and "(empty)" stay distinct.** An unset row is a prompt nobody has
  answered; a recorded empty value is a §11 fact ("checked, and it was blank").
  Collapsing them would put an assertion in the trail nobody made.
- **Nothing is back-filled.** An unset key is still ABSENT on the instrument, not
  written as an empty attribute.
- **Typing a key here still does not add it to the PROFILE.** Profile keys are
  administered in Configuration precisely so one operator's spelling cannot become
  a prompt on every other instrument.

The card counter now reads "Attributes (N set)" — it counts what is recorded, not
the prompts listed beside it.

## [Unreleased] - Instrument page: connection card, profile edit, token mask (2026-08-19)

Three operator-requested changes on the instrument pages.

- **The Connection card is SUPER_ADMIN only.** It is the device-wiring runbook —
  broker host, topic scheme, paste-ready publish command — and commissioning is a
  super-admin job here. Gated in BOTH places it appears: the card on the
  instrument detail page, and the "How this instrument connects" block inside the
  token dialog (which opens from creation and from regenerating a token, so
  gating only the card would have left the same content reachable). The token
  itself is not gated with it — whoever just issued it must be able to copy it,
  and revealing it later is separately controlled by password + audit row.
  **Presentation only:** the panel renders from the API base URL and shared
  constants, so this removes the instructions from the page, not the endpoints.
- **The profile is no longer editable in the read-only view.** It was a live
  `<select>` sitting in the details list: choosing an option fired a PUT
  immediately, with no Save and nothing to cancel, on a page where every other
  field waits for Save. It now travels in the same draft and the same PUT as the
  rest of the edit form. `moveToProfile` removed.
- **The access token mask shows no character of the token.** It used to render the
  8-character non-secret prefix followed by bullets; for a short token that is
  most of the credential, and a field showing real characters does not read as
  masked. Now a FIXED-width run of bullets — fixed so the mask does not leak the
  credential's length. The prefix is no longer rendered anywhere in the UI, but
  `GET /api/instruments/:id` still returns it, so the short-token warning was
  reworded to say the disclosure is through the API rather than on screen.

## [Unreleased] - Per-instrument display precision (2026-08-19)

Decimal places for temperature and humidity now come from each INSTRUMENT's own
attributes (`temp_decimals` / `humid_decimals`) instead of one site-wide number.
`0` shows whole numbers, `1` one decimal, and so on, everywhere the reading
appears. Precision belongs to the device: a probe resolving to 0.1 °C and one
reporting whole degrees sit in the same table, and any single number misreports
one of them.

- **`@digilog/shared/telemetry-decimals`** — `parseDecimalsValue`,
  `resolveDecimals`, `clampDecimals`, `formatDecimals`. Shared because the API
  resolves it, the web app formats with it and the alarm evaluator freezes it;
  two implementations would let one instrument render at two precisions.
  `"0"` is zero (not "unset"); `""` falls back; `"2.5"` / `"two"` are refused
  rather than rounded; every count is clamped before `toFixed`, which throws a
  RangeError outside 0…100 — a throw inside the floorplan's `.map()` would blank
  the whole dashboard over one stray attribute.
- **`telemetry-slots` config** — the two "decimal places" numbers become
  "— default" (used only when the instrument declares nothing), and two new
  ORDERED ALIAS LISTS name the attribute keys, matching the `alarm-limits`
  precedent for keys this install's operators type by hand.
- **Resolved server-side.** `GET /api/instruments/telemetry-overview` rows gain
  `decimals: { temperature, humidity }`; room-history series gain `decimals`;
  `GET /api/instruments/:id/telemetry` readings gain `slot` + `decimals`, so the
  raw key/value list on the instrument page agrees with the dashboard.
- **Surfaces** — tabular view (actual AND set point), floorplan chips + their
  aria-labels + the unplaced tray, room detail, the time-series chart (last-point
  label and hover readout, per series), instrument-detail latest readings, the
  alarms table, and ALARM_RAISED / ALARM_CLEARED notifications. Chart Y-axis ticks
  deliberately keep `niceScale`'s own rounding: a tick is a scale value, not a
  reading.
- **Alarms freeze it.** `ruleSnapshot.decimals` is written at raise time and read
  back by the alarms page and the clear notification. Editing an instrument's
  `temp_decimals` today must not re-render a closed §11 excursion at a precision
  nobody saw. Rows raised before the field existed fall back to the default.

**Fixed on the way (pre-existing, affects every config def):** the dynamic config
page seeded its form from the stored row alone, so any setting ADDED to an
existing def rendered as an empty field — and saving persisted the blank. For a
key-mapping setting that is silent: the mapping resolves to no keys and the
feature stops working behind a green save. Defaults now merge UNDER the stored
value.

**Not done:** nothing is back-filled. No instrument in `compliance_core_db`
declares either attribute yet, so every reading renders at the site default until
one is set per instrument.

## [Unreleased] - Instrument-limit alarms (2026-08-17)

Alarms raised from each instrument's own High/Low Temperature and Humidity Limit
attributes, in addition to the existing rule-driven alarms.

- **`alarm-limits` config** (super admin) — an ORDERED ALIAS LIST per bound saying
  which attribute keys carry the limits, because this install's keys have already
  drifted (`High Temperature`, `Low Temperature` and `Low Temperature Limit` all
  exist). Plus severity, a master switch, and the four status wordings.
- **Schema** — `Alarm.ruleId` nullable, `source` (RULE | INSTRUMENT_LIMIT),
  `limitKind` (HIGH | LOW), `clearedValue`. Enums 11 → 13. Migration
  `20260817090000_instrument_limit_alarms`, hand-authored, drift guard PASS,
  applied to `compliance_core_db_test` as well. A second migration the same day,
  `20260817120000_alarm_limit_unique_active`, adds a partial unique index
  (`alarms_active_instrument_limit_unique` on `instrument_id, metric, limit_kind`
  WHERE `state = 'ACTIVE' AND source = 'INSTRUMENT_LIMIT'`) so two overlapping
  evaluator passes can no longer both insert an open alarm for the same
  instrument/metric/bound.
- **Worker** — a second pass in `alarm-evaluation.worker.ts`, reusing
  `buildTelemetryOverview()` so telemetry-key resolution cannot drift from the
  dashboard. Identity is `(instrument, metric, limitKind)`.
- **Alarms page** — Instrument, Type, Severity, Raised, Value, Limit, Cleared,
  Cleared value, Status, Acknowledged. The Limit column reads the FROZEN snapshot, never the live
  attribute. A banner names instruments with no usable limits, so an empty page
  cannot mean both "all in spec" and "nothing is being watched".

**Deliberate decisions:** boundaries are IN spec; a blank or non-numeric limit is
NOT zero; an inverted high/low pair fires nothing; a MISSING reading neither
raises nor clears an instrument-limit alarm — it holds an open alarm, because
absence of data cannot prove recovery; room limits still colour the dashboard
and raise nothing.

**Known limitations:** an instrument-limit alarm can stay ACTIVE indefinitely if
its limit attribute is renamed, deleted, or inverted while the alarm is open —
there is no surface to retire it. The pre-existing RULE alarm path
(`decide.ts:83-88`) still clears on a missing reading; that defect was fixed only
for the new instrument-limit path, not for rules. The rendered UI has **not**
been visually verified in this session — browser automation on this machine is
blocked by MDM policy, not by the certificate; see the operator verification
checklist in `tasks/todo.md`.

**No permission, privilege, reauth or sidebar change.**

## [Unreleased] - Functional Locations: browse cards + detail page (2026-08-16)

Frontend only. No API, schema, permission or shared-package change - every endpoint
used already existed (`GET /`, `GET /:id`, `GET /linkable-instruments`,
`PUT /:id/instruments`).

The page was one flat list that doubled as the editor, with the instrument panel
appearing underneath whichever row was selected. It is now two views:

- **`/functional-locations`** - one card per **Block**, its Areas as clickable rows
  inside it. Deliberately not a flat grid of every location: a Block's count is a
  roll-up (own + all its Areas') and an Area's is its own, so side by side the two
  numbers would look like the same kind of number. Card shows `N in total` over
  `M linked directly - K areas`. Plus a search box (a Block stays in the results when
  an Area inside it matches), a real empty state, and loading skeletons.
- **`/functional-locations/:id`** (new route, `routes/functional-locations/detail.tsx`) -
  the location's details and its connected instruments. Breadcrumb to the parent Block,
  type badge, three stat tiles, the Areas grid, the editable instrument panel, and -
  for a Block - a **read-only** "Instruments in this block's areas" section.

**Why two instrument sections and not one:** `GET /:id` resolves the whole SCOPE
(own + every Area's) while `InstrumentPanel` lists only the DIRECT links. That
difference is not a bug and the panel must not change: `PUT /:id/instruments` sets
membership wholesale, so surfacing an Area's instrument in the editor would let an
unlink silently MOVE it up to the Block. They are rendered as separate, separately
labelled sections instead.

**Rename became Edit.** The shared dialog renders a live "Belongs to Block" picker for
an Area, but the old page's PUT sent `{ name }` only - so an operator could change that
picker, get a success toast, and find the Area still under its old Block. The detail
page now sends `parentId` too (the API already supported re-parenting and audits both
paths), and the dialog is titled "Edit functional location".

Edit / Add area / Delete moved onto the detail page; Delete navigates back to the
list on success and still surfaces the API's 409 verbatim ("still holds 3
instrument(s)"). A 404 from `/:id` (deleted in another tab, hand-typed id) renders an
explicit panel rather than a blank shell.

Routes in `main.tsx`: 48 -> **49**.

## [Unreleased] - Alarm subsystem (2026-08-13/14, project C)

Rules the evaluator checks every minute, the alarms they raise, and the e-signed
acknowledgement that answers for them. Phases C1-C3; C4 (notifications) is open.

### C1 - rules, evaluation, lifecycle

`AlarmRule` + `Alarm` models (migration `20260813164500_alarm_subsystem`, hand-authored,
drift guard PASS). Decision logic is pure and tested: boundaries are IN spec, a missing
reading is NOT a breach, and a rule with no usable threshold NEVER fires. The
`alarm_evaluation` worker runs per minute, registered in **both** `app.ts` and
`packages/queue/crontab.txt` in the same commit - a cron identifier with no handler
leaks jobs forever.

### C2 - acknowledgement

`POST /api/alarms/:id/acknowledge`: a reason (5-500 chars) plus `ACKNOWLEDGE_ALARM`
re-authentication, an `ALARM_ACKNOWLEDGED` audit row, and **409 on a second attempt** so
the first signature stands. The claim uses `acknowledgedAt: null` in the WHERE, so two
simultaneous requests cannot both succeed. The lookup is visibility-scoped: an alarm on
an instrument the caller may not see is 404, never 403.

- **No shared-package change was needed.** `ALARM_ACKNOWLEDGED` and its template were
  already present, RETAINED per 21 CFR when the previous alarm subsystem was torn out in
  Phase 6. Re-adding them was a duplicate-key tsc error.
- **`audit_trail.signature_meaning` is VARCHAR(255) while `reason` is TEXT.** An
  over-long reason acknowledged the alarm and *then* threw inside `auditLog`, leaving a
  regulated action with no audit row. Reason is now bounded in the body schema and every
  signature line in the module is clamped - including the three rule-CRUD lines from C1,
  which had the same latent overflow through a long rule name.

### C3 - UI

- **Alarms page** (`/alarms`): Active / History tabs that split on the CONDITION, with
  acknowledgement as its own column. A cleared-but-unacknowledged alarm - the overnight
  excursion nobody saw - must not read as finished.
- **Acknowledge dialog** collects the reason and the password TOGETHER, restating the
  alarm being signed for. Splitting them would let someone type a reason, get a password
  box, and no longer see what they are signing.
- **Alarm Rules config page** (`/config/alarm-rules`) with a card on Configuration. The
  condition text is rendered SERVER-side so this page and an alarm row cannot drift.
  A rule that has raised alarms cannot be deleted (RESTRICT); the 409 names the count and
  the row offers deactivation instead.
- **Dashboard Alarms card** - the one project B left absent. Top level only: it is a
  destination, not a drill-down. **Gated on the `alarms.view` permission ONLY**, not on
  the `dashboard-cards` config like the table and floorplan surfaces - so an admin
  hiding cards per role cannot hide this one. Adding an `alarms` key to that def is a
  follow-up, alongside the four already-inert keys noted below.
- Registry: 4 permissions (38 -> 42), 2 reauth actions (44 -> 46), 1 sidebar item
  (11 -> 12), an 11th `PERMISSION_TREE` group, and 4 configurable nodes (34 -> 38). The
  two alarm-rule nodes live under **Configuration**, not Alarms, because Alarm Rules is a
  config page - putting them in the Alarms group would make granting rule management
  light up the Alarms sidebar item. New ids must also join
  `CONFIGURABLE_PRIVILEGE_ORDER`, which drives membership of `FEATURE_TO_PERMISSION_MAP`.

### C4 - notifications

`ALARM_RAISED` and `ALARM_CLEARED` added to the `NotificationEventType` enum (migration
`20260814090000_alarm_notification_events`, hand-authored - `migrate diff` again emitted
the same three destructive statements, all stripped; drift guard PASS). The evaluator
enqueues a `notification` job on every raise and clear.

- **The `notification` queue handler was a STUB that discarded payloads.** Since the
  2026-05-17 rule-chain/alarm removal it logged whatever arrived and acknowledged it, and
  its own docstring asked for a real dispatcher mapping if a producer was ever wired back
  up. C4 is that feature, so the handler now dispatches. The drain behaviour is KEPT for
  non-event payloads: stale rows from before that removal may still be queued, and
  failing them would retry three times and park them forever.
- **Enqueued, not dispatched inline.** The evaluator runs every minute; a slow SMTP send
  inside the loop would delay detecting the next excursion. Producer-side failures are
  swallowed - the alarm is the regulated record and must not roll back because nobody
  could be told about it - while the CONSUMER lets failures throw so graphile-worker
  retries the delivery.
- An event type is described in **six** places (the Prisma enum, `EVENT_TYPE_META`, and
  `EVENT_LABELS` / `EVENT_FIELDS` / default email templates / default in-app messages in
  the dispatcher). All six are updated, and a test now holds `EVENT_TYPE_META`'s promised
  variables against what the payload actually produces - a variable advertised but never
  produced renders as an empty cell in the email an inspector reads.

### Test infrastructure fixed along the way

- `compliance_core_db_test` was **three migrations behind**; any e2e touching an
  instrument 500'd on a missing column. The test DB is migrated separately from the dev
  DB.
- `src/e2e/test-helper.ts` registers route modules independently of `app.ts` and had
  neither `functional-locations` nor `alarms`, so HTTP-level coverage of projects A and C
  was impossible to write. Both are registered now. `super-admin` is still missing, which
  is why `super-admin-unretire.test.ts` fails.


## [Unreleased] - Dashboard drill-down + instrument visibility (2026-08-13, projects B and D)

### B - Dashboard drill-down by functional location

Three levels: entry cards (All Instruments + one per Block) -> a Block's Areas -> the
Tabular / Graphical views scoped to the selection. Location dropdown in the header,
breadcrumbs back up, selection held in the URL (`?fl=`, `?view=`) so a scoped view is
linkable and Back walks up the tree.

- Cards are **data-driven**, not the eight names listed in the request - creating a
  location makes its card appear with no code change.
- Scoping is server-side through `resolveLocationIds()`, so a Block returns its own
  instruments **plus** its Areas'. `functionalLocationDirect` skips that expansion for
  the "direct" card.
- Welcome hero, Quick Overview and Quick Actions removed. **Four `dashboard-cards` keys
  are now inert** - `total_users`, `audit_trail`, `notifications`, `quick_actions`.
  They still appear on the config page and toggle nothing; removing them is a follow-up.
- **No Alarms card.** No alarm subsystem exists in this fork; it arrives with C.

Two bugs found only by looking, both now pinned by tests: the All Instruments card read
5 while its own view showed 20 (the tree counts only *placed* instruments - 15 of 20 are
unplaced), and "CWH - direct" said 1 instrument while showing 4 (the directOnly flag
never reached the query).

### D - Role and user instrument visibility

`instrument_scope` JSONB on **both** `role_configs` and `user_configs`, nullable with no
default so nothing is blinded when the migration runs. New Instrument Scope tab on
Config -> Roles & Access.

Proven against the live database (`apps/api/scripts/probe-visibility.ts`):

```
NULL unrestricted -> 20    [CWH] block+areas -> 4    [Module-E] -> 3
[Block C] -> 1             [CWH, Block C] -> 5       [] sees nothing -> 0
[stale id] -> 0            SUPER_ADMIN -> 20
```

- **`NULL` is not `[]`.** NULL inherits; `[]` means see nothing. Deliberately NOT the
  `length > 0` test `getMyConfig` uses - with three states, an emptiness test lets `[]`
  fall through to the role and turns a deny into a **grant**.
- **A user scope replaces the role's**, which is what "same role, different users,
  different instruments" requires. It can therefore widen as well as narrow; the role
  default is shown beside every override and each save is reauth-gated and audited.
- **A stale id contributes nothing** - a deleted location in a saved scope must never
  act as a wildcard.
- **Malformed JSON means inherit, not deny** - silently blinding a user is an outage
  disguised as a permission change.
- **Unassigned instruments are excluded** whenever a scope is active (SQL `IN` never
  matches NULL). Today that is 15 of 20.
- **`Prisma.DbNull`, not `JsonNull`** - the latter stores the JSON value `null`, a
  different thing, and the whole contract rests on the distinction.

Enforcement is on the query: the list merges visibility into the same `where` the count
uses so `total` cannot overstate; `GET /:id` applies it in the lookup and returns
**404, not 403**, because a 403 confirms the instrument exists; the overview **ANDs**
selection with visibility so picking a location outside your scope returns nothing
rather than overriding it. Administrative pickers are deliberately unscoped - organising
the estate is a different authority from viewing a subset.

Migration `20260813161500_instrument_scope`, hand-authored. Drift guard PASS.

## [Unreleased] — Functional Locations (2026-08-13, project A of four)

A sidebar feature for grouping instruments into a two-level **Block → Area** tree.
An instrument belongs to **at most one** functional location. This becomes the
authoritative logical grouping, superseding the free-text `block`/`area` columns.

Operator request covered four projects; this is **A only**. B (dashboard drill-down
with 3 entry cards and an FL filter), C (alarm subsystem), D (role/user instrument
visibility keyed to functional locations) each get their own spec. Spec:
`docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-13-functional-locations-design.md`; plan:
`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-13-functional-locations.md`.

### Added
- **Model `FunctionalLocation`** + enum `FunctionalLocationType` (BLOCK / AREA),
  self-relation for the tree, and `Instrument.functionalLocationId`.
  **31 → 32 models, 6 → 7 enums.**
- **Module `functional-locations`** (21 → 22) with 7 endpoints at
  `/api/functional-locations`: tree, one location, create, update, delete,
  `PUT /:id/instruments`, and `GET /linkable-instruments`.
- **Page `/functional-locations`** (45 → 46 routes): the tree with instrument
  counts, a create/rename dialog, and the Relation panel for linking instruments.
- **4 permissions** (38), **3 reauth actions** (44), **1 sidebar item** (12), a
  **10th PERMISSION_TREE group** with 4 configurable nodes (30 → 34), and 4 audit
  actions with templates.
- Migration `20260813154500_functional_locations`, hand-authored.

### Changed
- The free-text `Instrument.block` / `.area` columns are **superseded** — no longer
  read for grouping. **The columns are kept**, deliberately: a bad migration
  mapping must stay comparable and correctable. Dropping them is a follow-up once
  the tree is confirmed. `location` survives as descriptive text.

### Design notes worth keeping
- **Exclusivity is structural.** "An instrument in one location cannot be in
  another" is one-to-many, so it is a single nullable FK — the illegal state is
  unrepresentable rather than forbidden by a rule someone must remember. A join
  table would have permitted it and then needed a partial unique index to ban it.
- **Instruments may attach to a Block directly**, not only to an Area. The live data
  required it: `IOTGW_01` has `block = CWH` with no area, so an Area-only model had
  nowhere to put it. Consequently a Block's instruments are its own **plus** all its
  Areas', resolved by the single `resolveLocationIds()`. Querying
  `functionalLocationId = :id` directly silently omits the Areas — the likeliest bug
  in this feature, and why that helper exists.
- **Depth is capped at 2** and enforced server-side in `validation.ts`, not just in
  the form. An unknown id resolves to `[]`, never to every id, so a stale id cannot
  degrade into "no filter".
- **Delete is refused (409) while a location holds instruments or areas**, naming
  the counts. The FK is RESTRICT so the database would refuse anyway, but a
  constraint error is not something an operator can act on.
- **`@@unique([parentId, name])` does not make Block names unique** — Postgres
  treats NULLs as distinct. Service-layer check covers it; the SQL says so at the
  index rather than leaving a reader to assume.

### Migration result, verified against the live database
2 Blocks (`CWH`, `Block C`), 2 Areas (`Module-E`, `Sterile Core`), **5 instruments
linked, 15 left unlinked**:

```
CWH-01/02/03    [CWH/Module-E]         → Module-E
GWV-1785990849  [Block C/Sterile Core] → Sterile Core
IOTGW_01        [CWH/-]                → CWH   (Block, directly)
```

### Verification
api + web `tsc` clean, `vite build` clean, migration drift guard **PASS**, shared
suite at its 3-failure baseline, web suite at its 5-failure baseline (2 `use-can` +
3 `url-utils`, both pre-existing). Endpoints and the page were exercised in a real
browser: tree, counts, create, rename, delete-refusal, link, move and unlink all
confirmed with **zero console errors**.

## [Unreleased] — Instrument dashboard: table + drawn floorplan (2026-08-11)

Two dashboard views over the telemetry that was already being collected but had
nowhere to be looked at.

**Table view** — every instrument's current temperature and humidity, its room,
reading age and status, sortable and filterable. Fed by one new endpoint,
`GET /api/instruments/telemetry-overview`, which returns the whole fleet in a
single request rather than one call per instrument.

**Graphical view** — the floor DRAWN as SVG: each room a shape with walls, its
code, label, live readings and a status fill. Click a room for its instruments
and their live time-series, with the room's limits shown as an in-spec band and
a 15m/1h/6h/24h/7d window selector.

**The first cut showed the uploaded plan image with transparent hotspots over
it, and that was wrong.** On screen it read as a scan with rectangles stuck on
top — the rooms were invisible until hovered and the drawing's own ink competed
with the status colours it was meant to carry. The dashboard now draws the
layout and never renders the image; the image survives only in the editor, faded
behind the shapes being traced. Nothing behind the view had to change, because
rooms already stored proportional coordinates.

**Limits moved from the instrument to the room** — a documented reversal of the
2026-08-08 per-profile attribute keys. `Low/High Temperature Limit` and
`Low/High Humidity Limit` are retired from every profile's registration prompts.
A cleanroom's specification belongs to the room: replacing the probe on its wall
must not discard the spec, and two probes in one room must not be able to assert
two different specs. The `* Range` keys survive — those describe the device's
measurement capability, which genuinely is per-instrument.

**New:** 2 Prisma models (`Floorplan`, `FloorplanRoom`) + `Instrument.roomId`;
1 API module (`floorplans`); 1 config def (`telemetry-slots` — which telemetry
keys count as temperature and humidity, since ingest accepts whatever a device
sends); 1 config page (Floorplans placement editor); 6 audit actions and 2
reauth actions; `POST /api/uploads/floorplan`.

**"Live" is polling, not push.** This repo has no browser-facing WebSocket or
SSE channel, and the UI says "updates every Ns" rather than implying a stream.

**Two pre-existing bugs fixed on the way.** Profile photo upload read its token
from `localStorage.getItem('access_token')` — a key nothing in the app ever
writes, since the session token lives in sessionStorage under that name — so it
sent `Bearer null` and could never have worked; both uploaders now go through a
new `apiClient.postFormData()`. And the placement editor's own first version
pre-checked instrument boxes against a `roomId` field that `GET /api/instruments`
does not return, making every save a blind overwrite of the room's membership;
membership now comes from the plan-detail response.

**Migration notes.** `prisma migrate diff` wanted to `DROP TABLE
instrument_telemetry_history` (Prisma cannot express `PARTITION BY`, so it reads
the partitioned table as stray — it held 1180 rows) and to drop `NOT NULL` from
`audit_trail.chain_position`. Both were stripped from the hand-authored
migration; the reasoning is written into the SQL. Drift guard PASS.

The limit retirement is split: the migration edits only the registration
prompts, and `scripts/retire-limit-attributes.ts` does the audited move of
recorded values onto rooms. Deleting an attribute is a §11 record change needing
an attributable audit row, which raw SQL cannot write.

Spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-11-instrument-dashboard-floorplan-design.md`
Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-11-instrument-dashboard-floorplan.md`

## [Unreleased] — Per-profile instrument attributes (2026-08-08)

Each instrument profile now owns the list of attribute keys its New Instrument
form asks for. Nothing is shared between profiles.

**Amended the same day — a new profile starts EMPTY.** The first cut seeded a
new profile from the global list at Configuration → Instrument Attributes. In
use that failed the very purpose of the feature: the operator created a second
profile, saw the same twelve keys the first one had, and read the list as still
being global. Seeding is gone (`POST /api/instrument-profiles` now stores `''`
when `attributeKeys` is omitted), the "Default for new profiles" entry was
removed from the page's picker, and the `instrument-attributes` config key is
now **inert** — it seeds nothing and is asked for on no form. The key, its def
and its `GET /api/config/instrument-attributes/current` route were KEPT rather
than deleted: removing the config module is a separate decision that first has
to confirm the per-profile editor page does not lose its discoverability
through config auto-discovery / Configuration Access.

The cost is deliberate: Block / Area / Location are real placement columns, and
a brand-new profile does not ask for them until an admin adds them. The page
shows a per-profile amber advisory naming exactly which placement keys are
missing, which now fires on every new profile until its list is built.

This **reverses the "grouping only, nothing inherited" decision** recorded in the
entry below, taken the same day, and answers the question that decision deferred:
profiles inherit **prompts, never values**. No attribute on an existing
instrument is ever back-filled, rewritten or deleted because a profile's list
changed, and moving an instrument between profiles changes only which keys are
suggested — everything it has recorded stays and still renders.

The motivating case is concrete. This install's single global list held twelve
keys, of which seven were temperature/humidity limits and one a Modbus slave
address. No device needed all twelve, so every registration form was mostly
fields the operator tabbed past — and blank-but-asked-for is worse data than
never asked.

**`InstrumentProfile.attributeKeys`** (nullable `attribute_keys TEXT`), migration
`20260808163000_instrument_profile_attribute_keys`. The backfill copies the
**live** `system_config['instrument-attributes']` value rather than the
`INSTRUMENT_ATTRIBUTE_KEYS_DEFAULT` constant — this install's list is 12 keys and
the constant is 6, so seeding from the constant would have quietly reset every
profile to a list nobody configured. Day-one behaviour was therefore identical.
Drift guard PASS.

**Two states, not three.** A non-empty string is the profile's own list; `''`
*and* `NULL` both mean "asks for no attributes" — `parseInstrumentAttributeKeys`
returns `[]` for either, and no consumer falls back to the config key. (An
earlier draft of this entry claimed `NULL` fell back to the global template; it
never did, and with seeding removed there is nothing to fall back to.) The
editor cannot tell `''` from `NULL`, so any save on a `NULL` profile writes `''`.

**Configuration → Instrument Attributes has a profile picker.** It lists
profiles only and opens on the first one; every save is a `PUT` on the selected
profile. With no profiles at all the page says so and links to Instrument
Profiles instead of showing an editor with nothing to save. Switching profile
while dirty prompts before discarding, because the editor deliberately ignores
server revalidations mid-edit and an unsaved list has nowhere else to come back
from.

**A profile omitting Block / Area / Location now says so on screen.** Those three
are real placement columns, so instruments registered there get them empty and
the Instruments list Placement column and filters are blank for them. Advisory,
not a block — an accepted trade-off, chosen deliberately over pinning the
placement keys.

**The New Instrument form asks nothing until a profile is chosen**, and now tells
four states apart: no profile, loading, asks-for-none, and failed-to-load.
Previously a failed config read "simply yielded no attribute fields", which was
tolerable for a global blip and is not per-profile — it is indistinguishable from
a profile that asks for nothing, and the operator would register a device with
every attribute missing and no signal. A failure now says so and still does not
block registration.

**`attributeKeys` is exempt from `sanitizeStrings` on the profile routes.** The
two write paths for this same data disagreed: the dynamic-config `PUT` never
stripped HTML, while `stripHtml` *discards* tag-shaped content, so a key like
`Temp <5C` would have been kept by the Configuration page and truncated to `Temp`
by the profile page. An e2e test asserting a `<`-bearing key round-trips verbatim
is the guard.

**`GET /api/config/instrument-attributes/current` now has zero callers** — its two
consumers both read the owning profile instead. Kept deliberately and documented
as uncalled at the route, rather than left an undocumented orphan.

Audit records the **parsed key arrays** on before/after and names the count change
in `signature_meaning` (`… attribute keys changed (12 → 5)`), which fits its
`varchar(255)`.

**No count changed:** 29 models, 6 enums, 22 config defs, 102 permissions, 83
feature privileges, 92 reauth actions, 27 sidebar items. A nullable column is not
a model.

Spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-08-per-profile-instrument-attributes-design.md`.
Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-08-per-profile-instrument-attributes.md`.

## [Unreleased] — Instrument Profiles (2026-08-08)

Instruments are now grouped under named profiles: create a profile, then
register instruments inside it. `/instruments` is the profile list; the register
lives at `/instruments/profiles/:profileId` with its tiles, search and table
unchanged.

A profile is GROUPING ONLY — name and description, no settings, nothing
inherited. Adding inheritance later would raise "what happens to existing
members when the default changes?", which is a separate design question and was
deliberately left out.

> **Superseded later the same day** by the per-profile attributes entry above: a
> profile now carries one inherited setting, `attributeKeys`. The deferred
> question is answered there — profiles inherit prompts, never values.

**Membership is required, and existing instruments were backfilled.** Migration
`20260808120000_add_instrument_profiles` creates a `Default` profile and moves
every existing instrument into it, then makes the column `NOT NULL`. There is no
"unassigned" state for any code path to handle. Hand-authored, because
`prisma migrate diff` proposed an `ADD COLUMN NOT NULL` that fails outright on a
populated table — plus three unrelated changes it would have shipped: dropping
`audit_trail.chain_position`'s NOT NULL (weakening the tamper-evident chain),
`DROP TABLE instrument_telemetry_history` (32 rows, migration-managed but absent
from the datamodel), and churn on an unrelated FK. Drift guard PASS.

**A populated profile cannot be deleted, and the database enforces that.**
`ON DELETE RESTRICT` means no future code path can orphan an instrument or
destroy a group by accident; the endpoint's 409 exists to give the operator the
count and a next step, not to provide the safety. A test asserts both levels.

**The bulk CSV format did not change.** The profile is chosen once for the whole
upload, as a sibling field to `csv`, so template files already on disk keep
working.

No new permissions and no new reauth actions — profiles reuse `INSTRUMENT_*`.
Three audit actions were added: a profile RENAME changes what an inspector reads
against every instrument inside it. Moving an instrument between profiles rides
the existing `INSTRUMENT_UPDATED` row.

Found while building it, and fixed:

  * `INSTRUMENT_UPDATED`'s audit diff omitted `profileId`, so a move would have
    gone unrecorded. The existing test derives its key set from
    `updateInstrumentSchema.shape` precisely so that this fails — it did.
  * The instruments list was briefly filtered in the browser, which left the
    footer counting the unfiltered set: an empty profile announced "Showing
    1–10 of 15" over an empty table. Now a server-side `profileId` filter, so
    `total` is right and it scales.
  * `profiles?.data.find(...)` stops guarding at `profiles` — a body without
    `data` crashed the page. Hardened in three files.
  * "refuses a non-privileged role" posted an incomplete body, so Fastify's
    validation answered 400 and the assertion passed without the permission gate
    ever being consulted.

Prisma model count is now **29** (6 enums). The three CLAUDE.md files claimed
"61 models, 23 enums" — inherited from upstream DigiLog and never true in this
fork; the real count beforehand was 28 / 6. Corrected to verified numbers rather
than incremented from the stale ones.

Design + plan: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-08-08-instrument-profiles-design.md`,
`docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-08-instrument-profiles.md`.

## [Unreleased] — A local Active Directory to develop against, and two bugs it caught (2026-08-08)

There is no directory to develop against on this machine and none can be run —
Docker/WSL2 are unavailable here, ruling out samba-ad-dc or an OpenLDAP
container. `apps/api/src/test-support/fake-ad-server.ts` is an Active Directory
stand-in that speaks the real LDAP wire protocol (ldapjs, a new devDependency),
so the application talks to it through the unmodified `ldapts` client over a TCP
socket. It models the customer's layout: one parent group, five role sub-groups,
employees inside the sub-groups — and, crucially, the direct-vs-transitive
`memberOf` distinction, so the nested-group filter we recommend is genuinely
exercised rather than assumed. Run it standalone with
`npx tsx src/test-support/fake-ad-server.ts` to drive the real app in a browser.

`src/e2e/ldap-directory.e2e.test.ts` — **28 end-to-end tests** over that server:
auto-provisioning, all five group→role mappings, the two-bind flow, an
authenticated non-member being refused, `/api/auth/verify` succeeding with an AD
password, `enforceReauth` on a real endpoint, every refused password operation,
expiry exemption, the stranded-flag heal, role-mapping fallback, attribute sync,
and the failure modes (LDAP off, wrong service password, unreachable server).

Pointing the code at a real server immediately found two things mocks could not:

**`ldap://` never worked at all.** ldapts decides on TLS with
`secure = isSecureProtocol || hasTlsOptions`, so merely *passing* `tlsOptions`
forced a TLS handshake regardless of scheme. All three client sites passed it
unconditionally, so a plain `ldap://host:389` connection attempted TLS against a
cleartext port and failed with "Client network socket disconnected before secure
TLS connection was established" — an error pointing the operator at their
certificates when the real fault was ours. The config page offers `ldap://` in as
many words. Client construction is now centralised in `buildClient()`, which
passes `tlsOptions` only for `ldaps://`; `rejectUnauthorized` still defaults to
true there.

**Every first login bound to the directory twice.** The auto-provisioning path
authenticated and created the row, then the directory-user path authenticated the
same person again — four binds and two searches for one login, with the user's
password transmitted twice, and double the surface on which a flaky DC could fail
the login that provisions someone. `login()` now records that it provisioned this
request and skips the second round trip. Caught by asserting the exact bind log a
real server received.

Also fixed, found while driving the real UI: **every user's Edit page displayed
"Super Admin" as their role**, whoever they were. react-hook-form pushes the
user's role into the `<select>` when the user loads, but the options come from a
separate request that resolves later — setting a value for an option that isn't
rendered yet is a no-op, and the browser then falls back to the first option.
The save was never affected (RHF submits from its own state, verified by saving
a SUPERVISOR and re-reading the row), so this was a display defect rather than a
privilege escalation — but it told an admin the wrong thing on the one screen
where role is the point. Reproduced on both a directory and a local account.

Also fixed, found while stabilising the suite: `tcp-ingest` and `ws-ingest` each
polled with a `findMany` snapshot compared against a SEPARATE `count()`, so a row
landing between the two queries returned the empty snapshot — and since an empty
array is truthy, the poll reported ready and the next line dereferenced
`rows[0]` of nothing. Intermittent by construction; it surfaced as a different
ingest file failing on each full-suite run once the LDAP suite added load. Both
now derive readiness from the same rows.

## [Unreleased] — Active Directory integration made usable and safe (2026-08-08)

Written for a client who keeps one parent AD group containing five role
sub-groups (Admin / Supervisor / Operator / QA / Maintenance) with employee IDs
inside. Configuring that revealed the directory path had been carrying five
defects, three of them severe. LDAP login itself worked; **every other
credential surface had no idea directory users existed** and treated the
`LDAP_EXTERNAL_AUTH` sentinel as though it were a bcrypt hash.

**Re-authentication could never succeed for a directory user — critical.**
`authService.verify` and `lib/reauth-check.ts` both bcrypt-compared against the
sentinel, which never matches. An AD-authenticated Supervisor or QA could log in
but could not approve, sign, bypass, terminate, or save any reauth-gated
configuration — every 21 CFR §11.200 electronic-signature surface in the
product. Three attempts also locked the account. Both paths now re-bind to the
directory through the new `lib/ldap-identity.ts`, which is the single definition
of "is this credential ours?" that they share.

**Password expiry locked out every AD user after 90 days.** The expiry clock ran
on accounts whose password this application never changes, so `passwordChangedAt`
never advanced. At `passwordExpiryDays` after provisioning they were flagged
"must change password" — and the change-password screen cannot serve an account
with no local password. Exempted at login, in the per-request plugin gate, and in
the nightly notification sweep.

**"Reset Password" silently converted an AD account to local.** It hashed the new
password over the sentinel. The employee's AD password stopped working and —
worse — disabling them in AD no longer revoked their access here. Now refused,
along with self-service change, forgot-password (silently, to avoid a
user-enumeration oracle on a public endpoint), and approval of pending reset
requests. `unlock()` gained a password-free path so a locked AD account can still
be released without inventing a credential.

**A mapped role that did not exist created a permission-less ghost.**
`users.role` has no FK, so a mapping naming a role the application lacks — a
typo, or `QA` before anyone created it — produced a user who logged in
successfully to an empty application with no error anywhere. `resolveMappedRole`
validates against the Roles table, falls back to the default, and records both
names on the audit row (`mappedRoleNotFound`). `strictRoleMapping` opts into
failing closed instead.

**The config page silently disabled TLS verification.** Its `DEFAULTS` said
`tlsRejectUnauthorized: false` while the backend said `true`; the form seeds from
its own defaults before SWR resolves, so an admin who saved quickly wrote `false`
and re-introduced the on-path credential-harvesting exposure the backend default
exists to prevent.

**New — Access Restriction (`requiredGroups`).** Until now, restricting who could
sign in lived entirely in whether an administrator remembered to type a
`memberOf` clause into `searchFilter`; with the shipped default filter the whole
directory was admitted and auto-provisioned onto `defaultRole`, with no warning
anywhere. Now checked in code after the bind, using the same
whole-value-or-exact-RDN matching as `roleMappings`. Empty = unrestricted
(existing installs unchanged), and the page warns when it is.

Lockout for directory users is **delegated to AD** (operator decision): counting
locally as well produces double lockout, stranding an employee whose AD
credential is perfectly valid. Failures are still audited in full — only the
counter is delegated. The **User ID Format** config stays exempt for AD users, now
deliberately and test-guarded rather than by accident.

Users list and detail badge directory accounts and hide the local-password
actions the backend refuses; the unlock dialog no longer offers a temporary
password that would never be set.

Client-facing setup guide, including exactly what to request from the customer's
AD administrator and the PowerShell that produces it:
`docs/LDAP-AD-INTEGRATION-GUIDE.md`.

No schema change, no new permissions, no new reauth actions — all configuration
lives in the existing `system_config['ldap']` JSON.

New tests (30): `lib/__tests__/ldap-identity.test.ts`,
`modules/ldap/__tests__/required-groups.test.ts`,
`modules/ldap/__tests__/role-validation.test.ts`.

## [Unreleased] — Signal module removed; Instrument Activity promoted (2026-08-07)

`routes/instruments/signal.ts`, `signal-mast.tsx` and their test (300 lines)
are DELETED. The five-state freshness taxonomy they carried (live / due /
silent / heard / never, with a three-bar mast) was replaced by the two-state
Active/Inactive the operator asked for, and both pages had already stopped
importing them. Checked for references before deleting: none outside the files
themselves.

What survives the deletion, in `isInstrumentReporting` (@digilog/shared): the
per-instrument contract (judge against `expectedIntervalSec` where declared, a
configured window otherwise) and the slack multiplier that stops jitter
flipping a status. What is gone: the finer distinction between "overdue" and
"long silent", and between "never reported" and "reported but declares no
interval". If a finer status is wanted again the reasoning is in git history,
not lost.

`Instrument Activity` joins `Instrument Attributes` under Configuration →
Super Admin Settings. Listing it as a hardcoded card also removes it from the
auto-discovered "Additional Modules" section, so there is one door to it and
not two.

## [Unreleased] — Instrument ID accepts anything; the wire moves to UUIDs (2026-08-07)

**BREAKING for configured devices.** Every device must be reconfigured: the
MQTT client id and every topic segment are now the instrument's UUID. Retained
messages under the old code-based topics are abandoned.

`code` was `[A-Za-z0-9._-]`, max 64. It is now ANY characters, ANY length —
spaces, symbols, `<`, `>`, unicode, 200 characters if you like.

**The guard was not merely relaxed, it was replaced.** The charset existed
because the code WAS the topic segment: `/` forges a level, and `+`/`#` are
MQTT wildcards, so an instrument coded `+` would have matched the broker's
`instruments/${clientid}/...` ACL against EVERY instrument — read every
attribute downlink, publish telemetry attributed to any device. In a §11 system
that is forged records that read as genuine. So the code stopped being a topic
segment: `mqtt-auth-routes.ts` binds the client id to `instrument.id`, and
`attributeDownlinkTopic` / `childRosterTopic` / `parseTelemetryTopic` all carry
UUIDs. Nothing an operator types reaches a topic.

`etc/acl.conf` is UNCHANGED and needs no restart — `${clientid}` is whatever the
client presents, and the auth hook is what binds it.

Two consequences found by testing rather than by reading:

- **`audit_trail.signature_meaning` is `VarChar(255)`**, and a long code
  interpolated into "Instrument "…" registered" overflowed it — Postgres 22001,
  the create transaction rolled back, and the operator got a 500 for a legal
  instrument. The code is now truncated to 80 characters IN THE SENTENCE only;
  the full value is still recorded verbatim in the row's before/after JSON.
- **The HTML sanitiser was silently rewriting codes.** It strips anything
  tag-shaped, so a code of `<b>` was stored as the empty string. `code` and
  `name` are now exempt; every other text field is still stripped.

Verified live against EMQX 5.3.2 with an instrument whose code is literally
`+`: connecting with `+` as the client id is refused at CONNECT; connecting
with its UUID and subscribing to ANOTHER instrument's attribute topic gets no
SUBACK, a disconnect, and `authorization_permission_denied` in the broker log;
subscribing to its own topic gets SUBACK and receives its attribute downlink.

Still bounded, stated rather than hidden: the bulk-CSV importer splits on commas
and quotes, so a code containing either cannot arrive that way; and `code`
remains immutable after creation.

## [Unreleased] — Instrument attributes are collected at registration, from a configured key list (2026-08-07)

**New config def `instrument-attributes`** — 22 defs now (`ls apps/api/src/modules/config/defs/*.def.ts`; the "36" in CLAUDE.md was inherited from DigiLog and has never been true in this repo — corrected in the same commit). One setting, `keys`: a
textarea, one attribute key per line. The New Instrument form renders a field
per key and the person registering the device fills in the VALUES. Attributes
are free-form key/value pairs, which is right for the data model and wrong for
data entry — left alone, three operators store the same idea as "Room", "room"
and "Room No", and the register stops being filterable. The list is a PROMPT,
not a constraint: the detail page still accepts any key afterwards, and nothing
is back-filled onto instruments created before a key was added.

`parseInstrumentAttributeKeys` in `@digilog/shared` is the single definition of
what a line means — trimmed, blanks dropped, duplicates removed
case-insensitively (first spelling wins), capped at 25 so a runaway paste
cannot produce a fifty-field form. `GET /api/config/instrument-attributes/current`
is authenticated but not CONFIG_READ-gated: the people who register devices are
operators, and gating it would make the form silently ask for nothing for
exactly the role that fills it in.

**The form was trimmed** at the operator's request: no separate Name (the code
is sent as both — two identity fields is how half a register ends up named
after the device and half after the room), no expected interval, no Hardware
section. Block / Area / Location moved under the Attributes heading but remain
real columns, because the list page filters on them.

Attributes are written after the instrument POST returns, one call per key.
A failed attribute write does NOT discard the instrument: it already exists,
and its token is knowable only at that moment — the operator is told which keys
failed and can add them from the Attributes panel.

**"Instrument ID" now consistently means the CODE.** The detail page had been
showing `name` under that label while the create form used it for `code`, so
one name answered to two fields. The name field is gone from the edit form too.

## [Unreleased] — Child roster: a gateway is told who its children are (2026-08-07)

The attribute downlink announced a child only when that child *changed*. A
linked-but-untouched child was therefore invisible to its gateway, and
link/unlink published nothing at all — a gateway could not answer "which
instruments am I responsible for" from the broker alone. It now can.

**One retained slot per gateway**, `instruments/<gatewayCode>/children`, QoS 1,
carrying the whole membership: `{children: [{code, name, isActive}], ts}`. Whole
set, never a delta — the retained message is the only copy, and a gateway back
from a power cut must reconstruct the truth from it alone. Sorted by code so an
unchanged membership serialises identically. Inactive children are included and
flagged: dropping them would make a deactivated child indistinguishable from an
unlinked one, and those need opposite handling.

**A sibling topic, not a segment under `…/attributes/`.** Instrument codes allow
`[A-Za-z0-9._-]`, so a reserved segment inside that subtree could be collided
with by a real code. Cost is one extra subscription on the device.

**Republished on** link, unlink, move (both gateways), a child born linked, a
child deleted, and a child renamed or (de)activated — `name`/`isActive` are in
the payload, so an edit carrying no `gatewayId` still republishes its current
parent. A gateway created or promoted publishes its own (possibly empty) roster
at once, so "no children" is distinguishable from "the broker lost it".

**Cleared, not stranded.** Deleting a gateway, or turning gateway mode off,
publishes a zero-byte retained message. This is the only place in the codebase
that clears a retained slot, and deliberately so: unlike a stranded attribute
slot, a stranded roster names instruments that are still live and have just been
orphaned by that very delete.

The publish primitive was extracted from `attribute-downlink.ts` as
`publishRetained` and is shared, so both paths hold the SAME publisher
singleton — a second `setXPublisher` would need its own reset in
`test-helper.ts`, and the forgotten one would leak into the next app built in
the same process. Same guarantees as the attribute path: after commit never
inside it, membership re-read post-commit, never throws, silent no-op with
`MQTT_BROKER_URL` unset.

Two ACL rules added to `etc/acl.conf` above the `{deny, all}.` catch-all (below
it they match nothing, silently), and **the broker must be restarted** — EMQX
reads that file only at boot. Verified live against EMQX 5.3.2: a gateway
subscribing to its own `children` topic gets SUBACK and its roster; a different
instrument's valid token gets no SUBACK, a disconnect, and
`authorization_permission_denied` in the broker log.

## [Unreleased] — Destructive actions confirm in a themed dialog (2026-08-06)

Five destructive actions asked for confirmation through `window.confirm`:
remove instrument attribute, delete instrument, unlink a gateway's child, and
the notification-rules page's delete rule / delete group / delete template.
Every other confirmation in the app is a themed dialog, so the destructive
actions were the ones appearing in unstyled OS chrome — and `window.confirm`
blocks the JS thread, so nothing else on the page can react while it is open.

**New shared component** `components/ui/confirm-dialog.tsx`, following the
`audit-delete-dialog` idiom (red warning header, consequence in a red panel,
Cancel + a red confirm naming the act). `warning` is optional: the two
instrument cases have a real consequence to spell out, the notification-rules
ones mostly do not, and inventing red copy for those would train operators to
skip the panel where it matters. The template warning is the exception and was
verified against `notification-dispatcher.ts` — a rule pointing at a deleted
template keeps sending, falling through to the event's built-in default
wording.

**Two in-flight guards that did not exist before.** Deleting an instrument had
none at all: the button stayed live during the request, so a double click sent
a second DELETE and the operator got a spurious 404 toast for a row that had
just been removed. The three notification-rules deletes were likewise
unguarded. All six now disable both buttons and block backdrop/Esc dismissal
while the request is in flight, and close only once it settles — closing first
would leave the operator looking at a row that is still there if the call
failed.

Cancel is unchanged in effect and now has tests: the row button only opens the
dialog. Verified live against the broker on the attribute case — cancelling
publishes nothing, confirming publishes the `changed: {key: null}` downlink.

Not touched: the three notification-rules deletes still have no error handling
(a failed DELETE rejects as it always did, and the dialog stays open, which is
the honest outcome), and `alert()` survives elsewhere on that page.

## [Unreleased] — Attribute downlink: the first platform → device path (2026-08-06)

**This narrows a documented exclusion.** Spec
`2026-08-04-instruments-inbound-ingestion-design.md` §10 listed "Commands *to*
devices (downlink/RPC)" as out of scope for v1, and until now every transport
was uplink only. Changing an instrument's attribute is now published to the
device over MQTT. The exclusion is narrowed, not lifted: there is still no RPC,
no command channel, and no device→platform acknowledgement — attributes are the
only thing that travels this way. Recorded in a new spec §10.1.

**One retained slot per instrument.** `instruments/<code>/attributes`, or
`instruments/<gatewayCode>/attributes/<childCode>` for a child, which has no
broker connection of its own and must be addressed through the gateway that fans
out for it. Per-instrument topics are load-bearing: MQTT retains only the *last*
message per topic, so one shared gateway topic would mean a reconnecting gateway
receiving one child's state and losing the rest.

**The payload carries state and delta together** — `attributes` is the complete
current set (so a retained message alone is enough to reconstruct truth),
`changed` is this operation's delta, and `changed[key] === null` means the
attribute was *removed*: absent from `attributes`, null in `changed`, in the
same message.

**The database stays the source of truth.** QoS 1, retained, published only
*after* the transaction commits — publishing first would let a rolled-back edit
leave a device holding a change the platform does not have, and a retained one,
so it would survive. A publish failure is logged loudly and never fails the
attribute write. With `MQTT_BROKER_URL` unset there is no bridge and no
downlink, and attribute edits behave exactly as before.

**Devices gained their first subscribe permission.** `etc/acl.conf` previously
granted them none at all. Two rules were added: the bridge may publish on
`instruments/+/attributes` and `instruments/+/attributes/+`, and a device may
subscribe to `instruments/${clientid}/attributes` and
`instruments/${clientid}/attributes/#`. The `${clientid}` template is only
meaningful because the auth hook already refuses any CONNECT whose client id is
not the token's instrument code — the same binding that makes the telemetry
publish rule real. A gateway's client id *is* the gateway code, so the wildcard
form covers its children and nothing else. Verified live: a device reads its own
slot and its children's, and is disconnected when it reaches for another
instrument's.

**Retention had to be moved to disc.** EMQX 5.x defaults to
`retainer.backend.storage_type = ram`, which silently defeats the design — a
broker restart erased every slot, and a device reconnecting afterwards received
nothing at all until someone next edited an attribute on it. Verified, then
fixed in `etc/emqx.conf`.

**Known gap, not fixed:** a retained message outlives what it describes.
Deleting an instrument, or unlinking/moving a child, strands a slot that nothing
clears. No secret is exposed (only the instrument's own client id can read it),
but the data is stale. Clearing requires a zero-byte retained publish.

Full operator documentation, including a pasteable `mosquitto_sub` command:
`LOCAL_SETUP_WINDOWS.md` §9B.6.

## [Unreleased] — Instrument access tokens can be read back, and instruments carry free-form attributes (2026-08-06)

**This reverses a documented security decision.** Spec
`2026-08-04-instruments-inbound-ingestion-design.md` D5 said a device token is
stored hashed and shown once, because a retrievable credential is a standing
liability. That reasoning was not wrong; it was outweighed, at the operator's
explicit request, by what the alternative actually costs — a site visit to
reconfigure a device every time somebody needs to know what its token is. D5's
original rationale is preserved verbatim in the spec, with the reversal and its
compensating controls recorded beside it in a new §3.1.

**The hash is still the only thing authentication consults.** Tokens gained a
*second* stored form: AES-256-GCM ciphertext in `instrument_credentials.token_encrypted`,
alongside the unchanged SHA-256 hash. Nothing ever authenticates by decrypting.
The column is nullable on purpose — every credential issued before this change
has no ciphertext and stays unviewable rather than breaking — and ingest keeps
working with no key configured, with a wrong key, or with the ciphertext nulled
out. All three are asserted. The key is `INSTRUMENT_TOKEN_KEY`; rotating it
orphans existing ciphertext (reveals start failing, devices keep working), which
is documented next to the variable in `.env.example`.

**Three compensating controls pay for the retrievability**, and removing any one
re-opens the liability: encrypted at rest, `INSTRUMENT_UPDATE` plus a password
re-auth, and an `INSTRUMENT_TOKEN_VIEWED` audit row written inside the same
transaction as the read. The audit row is the one that matters — the token stays
secret, but who looked at it never is. Audit rows carry the prefix only; the
value is never logged, and both audit tests serialise the whole row and assert
the token appears nowhere in it.

**The re-auth is always-on, not admin-configurable, on all three token
endpoints.** This took two corrections in one day and is worth stating plainly.
Reveal and set shipped on `enforceReauth`, which consults
`system_config['action-reauth']` — and a stock install lists nothing there, so a
deployment that never opened the policy page had two of the three controls, not
three, with no way to tell from the outside which kind of install it was. A
control the reversal depends on cannot itself be opt-in. `POST
/:id/regenerate-token` was then left behind as pre-existing, which was the wrong
call: it returns a usable plaintext credential in its 200 body and is the *most*
destructive of the three, since it kills the credential the field device is
currently using. All three now use `enforceReauthAlways`.

Consequently `REVEAL_INSTRUMENT_TOKEN`, `SET_INSTRUMENT_TOKEN` and
`REGENERATE_INSTRUMENT_TOKEN` are all **absent from `REAUTH_ACTIONS`**
(40 → 39 actions). Everything in that registry is a per-role policy toggle; an
always-on gate has no policy, so an entry would render a control that changes
nothing whether on or off — the same "reauth theater" the three `*_TEMPLATE_KIND`
entries were deleted for on 2026-07-04, and the reason
`TOGGLE_SUPER_ADMIN_API_ACCESS` was never listed either. That left the
`Instruments` reauth category with no members, so it was dropped from
`REAUTH_ACTION_CATEGORIES` (8 → 7) along with the two per-category style maps in
the web app that are typed against it, and `PERMISSION_TREE`'s `instruments.edit`
node lost its `reauthAction`, which drove a policy badge for a policy that no
longer exists. The action strings still travel in the 401 bodies. **No new
permissions** — all three reuse `INSTRUMENT_UPDATE`.

`PUT /:id/token` sets an operator-chosen value, for the device whose credential
is fixed in firmware or on an installer's config sheet. `[A-Za-z0-9._-]` only,
so it survives an `Authorization` header, an MQTT username, a CSV cell and a
JSON line unescaped.

**Any length is accepted above one bound, and that bound is not about strength.**
This shipped with a 32–128 range, floored because `token_hash` is a fast SHA-256
and a short hand-typed token is genuinely brute-forceable. The bounds were
removed the same day at the operator's request: the endpoint exists for hardware
that dictates its own credential, and a limit the hardware violates cannot be
satisfied by arguing with the hardware. That reasoning was outweighed, not
refuted, and nothing about issuance changed — `generateToken()` still mints 43
base64url characters, so every token the system chooses for itself is still 256
bits.

What survives is a floor of `TOKEN_PREFIX_LEN + 1`, and it exists to keep a
*different* control honest. `instrument_credentials.token_prefix` is the first 8
characters, treated as non-secret: it is returned by the `INSTRUMENT_READ`-gated
list and detail endpoints and rendered on both instrument pages. At 8 characters
or fewer the prefix **is** the token — so a viewer who cannot reveal tokens would
read a live credential straight off the screen, with no password and no
`INSTRUMENT_TOKEN_VIEWED` row, bypassing all three controls above. The 32-char
floor had been covering that hole incidentally; removing it without this would
have opened it. `TOKEN_PREFIX_LEN` moved to `@digilog/shared` so the slice and
the bound cannot drift apart — deriving the prefix from a hash instead would be
the better fix, but `resolveInstrumentByToken` recomputes it on the presented
token, so changing the derivation would stop every existing credential matching.

It **revokes and inserts**
rather than updating in place, exactly as regeneration does:
`instrument_credentials` answers "which secret was live when this reading
arrived?", and rewriting a hash in place would make past readings appear to have
been authenticated by a credential that did not exist yet. A token already live
on another instrument is refused (409) — a duplicate would make authentication
ambiguous, since resolution seeks on the 8-char prefix and returns the first
matching hash. Concurrent claims are serialised on a per-token advisory lock.

**Free-form attributes** (`instrument_attributes`) are a child table, not a JSONB
column, so each change gets its own audit row naming the key and both values —
an attribute may hold a calibration date, which makes the change a §11 record.
Unique on `(instrument_id, key)`, cascading on instrument delete. `POST` upserts
(201 create / 200 update); `PUT /:key` deliberately does **not** create, because
a mistyped key on an edit is a typo and silently adding a second attribute beside
the one the operator meant to change is the failure that is hard to notice and
hard to undo.

**UI.** The instrument detail page gains an Access token panel — Reveal (with a
copy affordance and an on-screen note that the view was recorded), Set, and
Regenerate — and an Attributes table with inline add/edit/delete. The revealed
value is held in route-local state, never SWR: that is what re-hides it when the
operator navigates away, which is the difference between this feature and a live
credential left on screen at an unattended shared workstation. It flows into the
connection panel's Token/Username rows *and* the paste-ready command, which stays
runnable — verified by pasting the displayed `curl` into a terminal and getting
`{"accepted":2}`. A credential the API reports unrecoverable shows that plainly
and offers Regenerate instead of a Reveal button that could only produce an
error. Four places that told operators a token "cannot be retrieved" were
corrected; left standing they teach an operator to regenerate a lost token and
needlessly kill a working device.

**A guard against a bug that shipped three times.** An audit template's
placeholders are substituted in `apps/web/src/routes/audit/audit-helpers.ts`, and
nothing links the two files — so `{instrument}`, `{gateway}` and `{attribute}`
each reached the Audit Trail as literal text before being fixed reactively.
`routes/audit/__tests__/template-placeholders.test.ts` now walks
`AUDIT_TEMPLATE_DEFAULTS` at runtime and asserts no literal `{name}` survives
rendering, so a new template with an unhandled placeholder fails a test instead
of reaching an inspector.

## [Unreleased] — Every protocol the UI advertises now has a listener behind it (2026-08-06)

The Instruments detail page has always offered seven transports. Exactly one of
them worked. A technician could open the MQTT tab, copy a paste-ready
`mosquitto_pub` line, run it, watch it appear to succeed, and then spend an hour
debugging a device that was talking to nothing — because there was no broker
subscription, no socket server, and no upgrade endpoint. An amber "not accepting
connections yet" banner was the only thing standing between that page and a
support call. This lands the missing listeners so the banner can come down
honestly.

The design decision that made four listeners affordable was made first, before
any of them: the entire ingest pipeline — parse, gateway fan-out, dead-letter,
batched write, last-seen stamp — was lifted out of the HTTP route handler into a
transport-agnostic `ingestPayload()`. A listener's whole job is now to obtain
bytes and obtain a token and hand both over. Nothing else about ingestion is
duplicated anywhere, so a fix to fan-out or dead-lettering is a fix for all seven
protocols at once, and the `transport` recorded on a dead-letter is stamped by
whichever listener actually accepted the connection rather than claimed from a
field the device asserted about itself.

**Raw TCP** listens on `INGEST_TCP_PORT` — unset by default, because a port
opening on an operator's machine during an upgrade is a surprise nobody asked
for. A byte stream carries no headers, so the first line must be
`{"token":"..."}` and every line after it is one reading. That framing is its
own pure unit with its own tests: framing bugs pass every normal test and fail
the first time a message straddles a packet boundary, or the first time a split
lands in the middle of a multi-byte character and a naive per-chunk
`toString()` quietly rewrites the JSON. A stream also arrives with none of the
protections a web framework gives for free, so the listener adds them by hand:
an *absolute* five-second deadline to authenticate (an inactivity timer is
useless here — a scanner dribbling one byte every four seconds would hold a slot
forever), a post-auth idle timeout, a 64 KB per-line cap checked both on emitted
lines and on the unterminated remainder, a global connection cap, and real
backpressure so one chatty device cannot issue unbounded concurrent writes out
of order. A malformed reading is dead-lettered and the socket **stays open**;
one bad line must not kill a working device.

**WebSocket** is `GET /api/ingest/v1/ws`, taking the token either in the
`Authorization` header on the upgrade or in the first frame. `wss` is not a
separate listener — TLS terminates in front of the same route — which is why
both are marked live together. This re-adds `@fastify/websocket`, removed as
dead code in 2026-07; the commit says so, to stop a future cleanup stripping it
again.

**MQTT** is the one that is not ours to run. The API is a subscriber against an
external EMQX broker, not a broker itself, and that raises a question a CONNECT
check cannot answer: a device authenticated at connect time could still publish
to another instrument's topic, and MQTT never tells a subscriber who published,
so there is no check the bridge could make. Enforcement has to be at the broker,
and it takes two legs that are only meaningful together. Ours is
`POST /api/ingest/v1/mqtt-auth`, the hook EMQX calls per connection: the
username is the device token, resolved through the same single authority every
other transport uses, and the client ID must equal that token's instrument code
or the answer is deny. The broker's leg is a topic ACL permitting publish only
to `instruments/${clientid}/telemetry`, with `no_match = deny`. Composed, they
